subtitulo: Replacing the ten words you overuse
descripcion: Advanced English is limited less by what the speaker does not know than by what they reach for first. *Very*, *good*, *bad*, *thing*, *a lot*, *nice*, *interesting*, *make*, *get* and *big* cover an enormous amount of ground badly. Replacing them forces retrieval of vocabulary already known but inaccessible under time pressure. This week the words are simply banned.

cuadroReferencia.titulo: The ten banned words and where to go instead
filas: Is there one stronger adjective? *very tired* → *exhausted*
Say what made it so — natives hear this as negative

ejemplos.texto: *It was bland rather than bad — just forgettable.*
*The sauce was rich without being cloying.*
*Rice is a staple there, not a side dish.*
*The prices were eye-watering for what arrived.*
*It's an acquired taste, and I haven't acquired it.*

notas: *Very + adjective* usually means a stronger single adjective exists.
Precision is not formality. *Bland* and *stodgy* are everyday words, just specific ones.
*Thing* is almost always avoidable and almost always worth avoiding in writing.

contraste.es: Spanish leans on *muy* + adjective exactly as English leans on *very*, and both languages have the stronger single word available. The habit transfers directly; so does the fix.
contraste.de: German sehr + adjective works exactly like very + adjective, and German also has the stronger single words (eiskalt – freezing). The habit transfers directly, and so does the fix.
contraste.it: Italian often intensifies with -issimo (bellissimo, stanchissimo), which tends to become very beautiful or very tired. English prefers a stronger single word (stunning, exhausted).
contraste.fr: French très or vraiment + adjective works like very + adjective, and French also has stronger single words (épuisé – exhausted). The habit transfers directly, and so does the fix.
contraste.pt: Portuguese intensifies with muito or -íssimo (cansadíssimo), which tends to become very tired. English prefers a stronger single word (exhausted).

errores: Swapping an overused word for an obscure one. *Comestible* is no improvement on *edible*.

es: *importante* rendered as *important* for size: *an important amount* instead of *a considerable* or *large amount*.
de: *spannend* rendered as *exciting* for every interesting topic, which overstates it: *an exciting report* instead of *an interesting report*.
it: *importante* rendered as *important* for size: *an important sum* instead of *a considerable* or *large sum*.
fr: *important* for size carried over: *an important sum* instead of *a considerable* or *large sum*.
pt: *importante* rendered as *important* for size: *an important amount* instead of *a considerable* or *large amount*.

traducciones.fr: date limite de consommation vs. date de durabilité minimale
traducciones.it: data di scadenza vs. termine minimo di conservazione
traducciones.pt: data-limite de consumo vs. data de durabilidade mínima

traducciones.de: so gut, dass man weiteressen möchte
traducciones.fr: irrésistible / qui donne envie d’en reprendre
traducciones.it: irresistibile / che invita a mangiarne ancora
traducciones.pt: viciante / que dá vontade de comer mais

mision.consigna: Write a review of a meal, a restaurant or a dish you cooked.
requisitos: the ten banned words appear zero times

microtareas.texto: Write ten sentences using the banned words, then rewrite each without them.
Describe one dish in five adjectives, none of them evaluative.
Record 90 seconds about a meal with the ban in force. Notice where you stall.

autochequeo: Search the text for each of the ten. Zero hits?
Any word precise but too obscure for the register?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on lexical precision. (1) Flag every banned word that got through. (2) Flag every vague adjective and give two precise alternatives. (3) Flag anything precise but too obscure for the register. (4) Say which three sentences are strongest and why. Do not rewrite the text.
